title: Heel turn
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 357. Public domain. Heel-turn construction widely described in Weldon's Practical Knitter (Victorian series). Public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: Rows that do not travel the full width of the work, used to create three-dimensional shaping such as a heel cup, dart, or shoulder slope.
Slip, slip, knit: two stitches slipped individually as if to knit, then knitted together through their back loops. Produces a left-leaning decrease.

content.text: The secret of the heel turn is that a series of
short rows

builds a three-dimensional cup from a flat strip. A decrease at each turning point joins the stitches left on hold, so no gap remains in the heel cup. The shape is surprising until you see it. Rows of decreasing length naturally curve the fabric around a corner.

You need a set of double-pointed needles or a circular needle, yarn appropriate for socks (fingering or 4-ply weight works well), and a basic understanding of working in the round and of slip stitches. The heel flap leading into the turn is usually worked flat on half the sock's stitch count.

attrs.title: Fig. 357, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
The example below uses a heel flap of 32 stitches (half a 64-stitch sock). Adjust the numbers proportionally for other stitch counts.
Set-up row (right side): Knit 18 stitches, ssk, knit 1, turn. Leave the remaining 11 stitches unworked on the left needle.
Wrong-side row: Slip 1 purlwise with yarn in front, purl 5, p2tog, purl 1, turn. Leave the remaining stitches unworked.
Right-side row: Slip 1 purlwise with yarn in back, knit to 1 stitch before the gap,
ssk
(knitting the stitch on each side of the gap together), knit 1, turn.
Wrong-side row: Slip 1 purlwise with yarn in front, purl to 1 stitch before the gap, p2tog, purl 1, turn.
Repeat steps 3 and 4 until all the held stitches have been consumed, ending after a wrong-side row. The heel cup is now complete.

Pick up and knit stitches along both sides of the heel flap to rejoin the instep stitches and resume working in the round. The number of stitches picked up per side will be roughly equal to the number of rows in the heel flap divided by two.
Where you'll see it

The heel turn with flap is the most common heel construction in top-down sock knitting. It appears in the vast majority of traditional sock patterns from Weldon's Practical Knitter onward and produces a reinforced heel cup suited to hard-wearing use. The same short-row logic without the flap is used in the flap-free or short-row-only heel construction favoured in toe-up socks.
Common faults

Holes at the turn points. If the slip stitch at the beginning of each short row is not tight enough, a visible hole forms at each turning point. Slip the first stitch firmly and work the decrease (ssk or p2tog) tightly into the stitch on each side of the gap.

Wrong stitch count at the end of the turn. The turn is complete when all the held stitches have been consumed. If stitches remain unworked, an extra row or two is needed. Counting 1 stitch before the gap and 1 after the decrease on each row keeps the count predictable.

Ladder at the pick-up join. After the heel turn, a loose column often develops where the heel stitches meet the picked-up side stitches. Picking up one extra stitch at each corner and working it together with the adjacent instep stitch on the first decrease round closes this ladder.
What to try next: once the heel turn feels easy, work the gusset decreases. These follow the heel turn and taper the foot back to the original stitch count over the next few rounds.
